title: “BY HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED” — THE VERSE WE QUOTE FOR SICKNESS WAS FIRST TALKING ABOUT SOMETHING EVEN MORE DEADLY
paragraphs: “BY HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED” — THE VERSE WE QUOTE FOR SICKNESS WAS FIRST TALKING ABOUT SOMETHING EVEN MORE DEADLY

Isaiah 53:5 is often spoken over hospital beds, cancer diagnoses, chronic pain, and bodies desperate for healing. God absolutely can heal the sick. But what if the wound Isaiah was ultimately staring at was deeper than the sickness in your body? What if the greatest miracle promised in this passage is the healing of something every human being desperately needs healed?
There are Bible verses we read.
And then there are Bible verses we reach for when our hands are shaking.
Someone you love is lying beneath hospital lights while machines make sounds you never wanted to understand.
And somewhere between fear and faith, someone whispers:
Maybe you have whispered it too.
Maybe you prayed it until your voice cracked.
Maybe you believed with everything inside you that the next scan would be clear, the next test would be different, the tumor would disappear, the pain would stop, the miracle would come.
We should never become so intellectually sophisticated that we explain away the God who created the human body and remains perfectly capable of restoring it.
Jesus healed the sick. The apostles prayed for healing. James tells suffering believers to pray. Christians have every biblical reason to bring sickness boldly before God.
But there is another side of this verse that we cannot afford to miss.
Because Isaiah 53:5 was never meant to become a slogan that makes a suffering Christian feel spiritually defective when the hospital room remains occupied.
And when you read the verse in its own language…
then keep reading the surrounding verses…
then watch how the New Testament itself interprets Isaiah…
You discover that “by His stripes we are healed” reaches deeper than the skin.
Isaiah is bringing us face-to-face with the sickness beneath every sickness.
And the Servant who would be wounded to bring sinners home.
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
A careful sense of the phrase is:
“And by His wound, healing has come to us.”
The Hebrew word often translated “stripes” is חַבּוּרָה — ḥabburah — carrying the idea of a wound, bruise, welt, or injury produced by a blow.
But do not isolate those words from everything Isaiah has just said.
So that peace might come to us.
Then Isaiah says that through His wound we are healed.
This is not primarily the language of a medical transaction.
It is the language of substitution.
Someone innocent is suffering because someone guilty needs peace with God.
And the guilty ones are us.
That is why the next verse matters so much.
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way…”
Isaiah does not immediately say, “All we like sheep became physically ill.”
That is the disease Isaiah is exposing.
The human heart walked away from its Shepherd.
And then comes one of the most astonishing statements in the Old Testament:
“…and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Because Christianity becomes meaningless when we make the cross merely an inspirational story about enduring suffering.
Jesus did not die merely to show you how much suffering a person could survive.
He was not simply history's greatest example of perseverance.
The righteous One stood where the unrighteous belonged.
The innocent suffered for the guilty.
The Shepherd was struck for wandering sheep.
Jesus Christ stepped into the courtroom carrying nothing deserving condemnation…
This is where “by His stripes we are healed” becomes far more uncomfortable than the inspirational quote printed on a coffee mug.
Because before you can celebrate the healing, you must admit the disease.
We were not merely wounded people needing encouragement.
Because our culture is comfortable saying, “I’m hurting.”
We are less comfortable saying, “I have sinned.”
We will talk about what people did to us.
And those wounds can be painfully real.
But Scripture also asks a question our generation desperately wants to avoid:
What have we done against God?
What has been happening inside you?
The affair hidden behind deleted messages.
The unforgiveness you keep calling “boundaries” even though deep inside you know hatred has been feeding there for years.
The Sunday worship with the Monday compromise.
The Bible verses posted publicly while private sin remains protected.
Maybe that is why this verse feels different when we stop treating it merely as a promise about circumstances.
Because Isaiah is not allowing us to stand at the cross pointing at everyone else's wounds.
He makes us look at our own sin.
he makes us look at Jesus.
This is where the story turns.
Because Christianity does not say, “Look how terrible you are; now fix yourself.”
Now look at what Christ did about it.
Centuries after Isaiah wrote those words, Peter reached back into Isaiah 53 while explaining what happened at the cross.
He wrote that Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness,” and then echoed Isaiah:
And Peter does something enormously important.
He tells us what kind of healing he has in view.
“For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.”
Peter himself connects the “healing” language with Christ bearing sin and wandering sinners returning to their Shepherd.
That does not make physical healing unimportant.
Because imagine receiving a perfectly healthy body…
What would you really have gained?
Jesus once asked what it profits someone to gain the whole world and lose his soul.
We might ask something equally sobering:
What good is a healed body if the soul remains unreconciled to its Creator?
Trust the God who raises the dead.
But never reduce the cross to a guarantee that every faithful Christian must experience immediate physical healing in this present life.
Because some extraordinary believers have prayed faithfully…
Timothy apparently experienced recurring physical problems.
The Gospel does not promise Christians exemption from mortality before the resurrection.
Death itself will not have the final word.
That is Christian healing in its ultimate horizon.
Christ does not merely patch up Adam's dying world.
There is coming a day when what Revelation describes becomes reality: death will be no more. Mourning will end. Crying will end. Pain will end.
Not because Christians learned the correct formula.
Not because they accumulated enough faith points.
for the Christian, complete physical healing is coming.
Sometimes God graciously gives us a foretaste now.
Sometimes doctors cannot explain what happened.
Sometimes recovery comes slowly through medicine, surgery, therapy, rest, and the ordinary providence of God.
and the answer we wanted does not come before death.
But resurrection means sickness still loses.
Cancer does not get the final sentence.
Alzheimer's does not write the ending.
Paralysis does not write the ending.
Chronic pain does not write the ending.
The cemetery does not write the ending.
And perhaps someone reading this needs that truth because you have been quietly blaming yourself.
And somewhere along the way you began wondering whether you failed.
Maybe you did not have enough faith.
Maybe you said the wrong prayer.
Maybe God was disappointed with you.
Isaiah 53:5 is not a weapon meant to beat suffering Christians with guilt.
It is a window into the suffering Servant who carried our guilt.
Jesus is not standing beside your hospital bed accusing you because you are still sick.
He knows what it is to groan.
He knows what it is to bleed.
And ultimately, He entered death itself.
The astonishing claim of Christianity is not that God watched human suffering safely from heaven.
God the Son entered our world.
And then Jesus walked out of the grave.
Maybe that is the image you need tonight.
The risen Jesus still bearing scars.
But the wound did not win.
And perhaps your story has scars too.
Some came from choices you made.
Some came from sins you still struggle to forgive yourself for.
There are chapters you would delete if life had an edit button.
There are nights you wish nobody knew about.
Maybe even Christianity you performed while your heart wandered far from Christ.
Could Jesus really want someone like me?
Isaiah 53 answers from seven centuries before the crucifixion:
That is exactly why the Servant was wounded.
Not people who almost had their lives together.
This is the scandal of grace.
And the resurrection declares that sin, Satan, condemnation, and death will not have the final word over everyone who belongs to Christ.
That is why grace is scandalous.
Because Jesus does not merely improve respectable people.
He takes stories that should have ended in shame and writes mercy across them.
Grace is not Jesus giving us permission to remain comfortably chained to the sins for which He died.
Peter says Christ bore our sins so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.
Jesus does not save us so we can proudly decorate our prison cells with Bible verses.
Repentance is not payment for salvation.
It is the turning of a heart that has finally realized the Shepherd is better than wandering.
Maybe that is your moment right now.
Not after you clean yourself up.
You may have opened this expecting an article about physical healing.
And somehow God has brought the conversation somewhere deeper.
Perhaps the healing you desperately need tonight begins with three words nobody around you can see:
There is no magic in repeating words.
Come to Christ with genuine repentance and faith.
Trust the One who bore sin on the cross and rose from the dead.
The person you became while everybody thought you were okay.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people can become slightly better.

It is the announcement that guilty sinners can be forgiven, wandering sheep can come home, enemies can receive peace with God, and spiritually dead people can receive life because Jesus Christ died and rose again.

And if Christ has already begun rebuilding a life you once thought was beyond redemption, tell someone what He has done. Your testimony might become the sentence God uses to interrupt another person's despair.
Not because an algorithm needs another save.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is only a religion for people who have their lives together.
Because perhaps they need to discover what we discovered in Isaiah 53.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of people who healed themselves.
It is the story of wounded sinners meeting a wounded Savior…
and discovering that His wounds were not the end of His story.
our wounds do not have to be the end of ours.
So the next time you hear someone whisper:
See the Servant pierced for transgressions.
See the punishment that brings peace falling upon Him.
See wandering sheep being carried home.
The greatest healing Isaiah promised was never merely about getting you out of a hospital.
It was about bringing you home to God.
Your sickness may have wounded your body.
People may have wounded your heart.
Sin may have devastated years of your story.
But if you belong to Jesus, none of those things gets to write your final chapter.
The scars may explain where you have been. Only Jesus gets to decide where your story ends.
